meta.description: DARWIN puts a coding agent to work on real artifacts — code, models, video — and keeps only the versions that pass the check. An evolution lab by RiseAI.

home.lede: DARWIN puts a coding agent to work on real artifacts — code, models, video — one round at a time. Tests and judges check every attempt. Improvements survive; every rejection stays on the record.

story.title: A higher score that still lost.
story.body: In the video run, round 3 scored 77 — above the 75.5 of the version being kept. But DARWIN also puts old and new side by side, in both orders. The new cut lost both times, so the earlier version stayed. The rejected cut is still there to watch.

story.caption: Scores explain a decision. They don't make it alone.

how.title: Variation, then selection.
how.intro: You define the goal and how to judge it. The agent varies the work; the judge selects. Only a better version moves forward.
how.s1d: Start from a draft and a fixed judge — tests, a metric, or a model jury. Inputs stay frozen for the whole run.
how.s2d: A coding agent edits only the allowed files, always starting from the best version so far.
how.s3d: The candidate runs in a fresh copy: tests execute, models train, videos render.
how.s4d: Better versions become real Git commits. Rejections and failures are saved, not hidden.
how.note: DARWIN improves the artifact, not the agent's weights. It doesn't claim general self-improvement.

log.title: Sixteen domains. One loop.
log.intro: Some runs improved a lot. Some didn't improve at all. All of them are here.

start.title: Start with one small task.
start.body: Install the package, pick a template, and let your own coding agent take the first rounds. Everything runs on your machine.

faq.title: Before you begin
faq.a1: No. You're looking at replays of finished runs — real artifacts, real scores, real decisions. Browsing never calls a model and needs no account.
faq.a2: No. Real runs plateau, fail and get rejected. DARWIN keeps those records next to the improvements, and the final artifact is simply the best version under that run's rules. Scores from different tasks can't be compared.
faq.a3: No. DARWIN improves the artifact — code, prompts, configs, guides — not the agent's model weights. It's a disciplined loop around tools you already use.
faq.q4: Can I use my own material?
faq.a4: Yes. Start from the closest template and swap in your inputs, draft and goal. Use material you're allowed to use, and start a new run whenever the inputs or the judge change.
faq.a5: The complete runs here used Codex. Adapters also exist for Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini, Qwen Code, Kimi, OpenCode, Copilot, CodeBuddy and Qoder, but not all are tested end to end. You bring your own login; each run records which model was requested and which one answered.

limits.code-speed: Historical run. Preprocessing may be reused within one batch of names, and timings depend on the machine and random inputs. Source was rebuilt from the original patches and passed an independent correctness check. Later re-measurements never replace the historical curve.
limits.code-repair: A synthetic Python expense project. Fixed tests check money precision, split remainders and monthly totals. The result only describes these fixed tests.
limits.cpu-classifier: The fixed validation set has 450 digits; training uses 1,347. The validation set was used repeatedly to choose a configuration, so this isn't evidence of generalization to new data. Rounds without a change have no formal score.
limits.video-cut: Footage is an excerpt of a historical speech marked public domain on Wikimedia Commons. The score mainly judges segment choice and structure from the transcript; audio, duration and decoding are verified separately. A text score isn't a full judgment of the viewing experience.
limits.svg-drawing: Scores come from one judge model looking at the rendered PNG, one sample per round, with whole-number criteria — coarse enough to cause run 1's plateau. Side-by-side comparisons use the same judge, two votes each (one per order). The scores describe this rubric only, not any model's drawing ability.
limits.landing-page: The product, prices and amenities are fictional. The judge sees a desktop and a phone screenshot plus the page text, one sample per round, so small gaps — like round 4's 72 against 72.5 — are within its wobble. Scores aren't conversion rates; have a person review a page before it goes live.

visual.run2_start: Run 2 starts from run 1's final drawing, with a new rule: ties are settled side by side.
visual.story_pelican: In run 1, rounds 3 to 5 each changed the drawing visibly, yet the judge gave the same four criterion scores every time. Each total was 75, and “the score must go up” rejected all three. Rules never change in the middle of a run, so a second run added ties: compare — a tied candidate goes to the same both-orders, side-by-side comparison. Ties can lose too: round 5 of run 2 lost 0/2.
visual.story_landing: Two earlier landing-page runs were scored on faulty phone screenshots: the lower part of the page rendered blank, and the judge rejected three rounds as a broken layout. The renderer was fixed and given a regression test, and this run started over. The case notes explain why the earlier runs were left out.

start.title: Run your first experiment.
start.lede: Browsing needs nothing. Running your own task needs Python 3.11, Git, and a coding agent you're signed in to.

install.title: Install the package
install.body: DARWIN ships as the rsi-anything Python package: the rsi command plus 18 templates. Install it into a fresh virtual environment.
install.note: rsi setup checks Python, Git and the coding agents you're signed in to, and suggests who should edit and who should judge. On native Windows, activate the environment with .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1.
install.private: The source repository isn't public yet. The package contains everything needed to run the templates.

run.title: Pick a small task
run.body: Each template ships with a draft, inputs and a judge. Get one working end to end, then swap in your own material.
run.shell: Run in a separate task folder
run.note: Replace YOUR_MODEL with a model your account can use. rsi check runs the real evaluator — templates with model judges make real calls. Run rsi init with no arguments to list all 18 templates.

results.title: Review it and take it with you
results.body: Artifacts and the full record stay in your task folder. Generate a report, then export a copy you can share.
results.resume: Interrupted? Resume with the same configuration. Changing the goal, the inputs or the judge starts a new run.

sources.title: Sources & licenses
sources.body: The loop is DARWIN's own implementation on Python, Git and PyYAML. Templates optionally use scikit-learn, Matplotlib, FFmpeg and PyTorch. Code is MIT licensed; data, media and models keep their own terms — the default backtest market data, for one, is non-commercial.
sources.limits: 14 domains have complete multi-round runs. Video generation is partially measured because the public service stopped responding; GPU kernels are waiting for a personal GPU.

pre.code-repair: Python tests only, no extra dependencies. All you need is a coding agent you're signed in to.
pre.code-speed: Uses local Python to check results and time them. Timings depend on your machine — start with the default task.
pre.cpu-classifier: Install the training dependencies from requirements.txt in the task folder. Runs on CPU.
pre.video-cut: Needs FFmpeg and ffprobe, a prepared video and transcript, and a model judge you can call. Prepare the footage as the template guide describes.
pre.svg-drawing: Needs a Chrome-family browser for offline screenshots and a judge that can read images, such as cli:claude. Start with the pelican, then swap in your own subject.
pre.landing-page: Needs a Chrome-family browser and a judge that can read images. The product is fictional; replace judge/brief.md and judge/facts.json with your own.

own.title: Or improve something of your own
own.body: rsi new asks what should get better — a text, a drawing or page, code with tests, or any number a command prints — and writes a task that runs as written: the contract, a judge and a starting file.
own.note: Rewrite the generated rubric in your own words before a serious run: the judge reads it literally. rsi setup suggests who should edit and who should judge.
